channel.title: Nicotine Science and Policy
channel.description: Daily digest of views, debates and discussions on nicotine science, policy, regulation and advocacy.

item.title: Survey finds proposed vaping restrictions could cost public health £4.5bn a year
item.description: Proposed vaping restrictions should be judged not only by their intention, but by their cost to public health. Hiding or limiting lower-risk products may reduce visibility, but it can also make switching less likely for adult smokers who still need a route away from cigarettes. A policy that discourages vaping while smoking remains available risks protecting the wrong behaviour. Regulation should target youth access and irresponsible retailing without weakening one of the most practical exits from combustion. (Published on September 04, 2026byconveniencestore.co.uk)

item.title: Nicotine E-Cigarettes for Cigarette Smoking Cessation: Recommendations to US-Based Clinicians
item.description: Clinicians now have stronger grounds to discuss nicotine e-cigarettes as part of smoking cessation care. The JAMA recommendations recognise that adult smokers need patient-centred advice on the full range of evidence-based options, including vaping where appropriate. That matters because misperceptions about relative risk can keep people tied to cigarettes even after repeated quit attempts. Medical guidance should be clear enough to help smokers move away from combustion, while still explaining limits, uncertainty and the need to switch completely. (Published on September 04, 2026byjamanetwork.com)

item.title: GFN.TV Interviews #95 | THEY DON’T COUNT | A GFN Dispatch From the Global War on Nicotine
item.description: “They don’t count” captures one of the deepest failures in nicotine policy. Smokers, vapers and users of safer nicotine products are often treated as statistics, problems or collateral damage rather than people whose choices determine whether harm is reduced in practice. A global war on nicotine can lose sight of the real target: disease and death caused by smoking. Public health should count the people it claims to protect, especially those trying to move away from combustion. (Published on September 04, 2026bygfn.tv)

item.title: Ending ‘Christmas for criminals’: Coalition's tobacco tax cut argument
item.description: Australia’s tobacco excise debate shows how quickly public health policy can become an organised crime opportunity. Extremely high taxes may be designed to discourage smoking, but they can also make illegal cigarettes profitable enough to sustain violence, corruption and a market beyond normal controls. Enforcement alone cannot fix incentives this large. A credible strategy should reduce smoking while keeping consumers inside legal channels and making lower-risk nicotine alternatives easier to access than illicit tobacco. (Published on September 04, 2026bypolitico.com)

item.title: Part One: From Pesticide to NRT: A Regulatory History of Nicotine
item.description: Nicotine’s history is far more complex than the way it is usually discussed. The same substance has been framed as poison, dependence driver, medicine and harm reduction tool, depending on dose, delivery and context. That matters because public health debates often flatten nicotine into a single moral category. Better policy starts by separating the substance from the smoke, the risk from the rhetoric, and the product from the purpose it may serve. (Published on September 04, 2026bysubstack.com)
